title: To the Right of the Cemetery There Is a Barren Field...
text:
To the right of the cemetery there is a barren field;

behind it, a river of sparkling blue.

You said: "Fine, go to a convent

or marry a fool..."


It was the sort of thing princes always say,

but they are words never forgotten.

Let a hundred centuries slide in a quarrel

like an ermine mantle beneath their shoulders.




1909
editorial_note: The translation keeps the remembered aristocratic dismissal and the long glide of time.

title: When in the Dark Night I Await Her Arrival...
text:
When in the dark night I await her arrival,

it seems to me that everything hangs by a thread.

What are honors worth, even freedom,

when she comes promptly and plays the pipe?

Look, here she comes! She throws aside her veil

and stares at me long and fixedly. I say:

"Was it you who dictated to Dante the pages about hell?"

And she answers: "I am she."
editorial_note: The translation preserves the apparition's authority as the force behind Dante's infernal vision.

title: They Arrived at Dawn and Carried You Away
text:
They came at dawn and took you with them.

You were my death: I walked behind.

In the dark room the children cried,

the blessed candle gasped.

Your lips were cold from kissing the icons,

sweat pearled your forehead: those mortal flowers!

Like the wives of the hosts of Peter the Great I

will stand

in Red Square and howl beneath the Kremlin towers.




1935
editorial_note: The translation keeps the arrest scene's funeral imagery and public vow of grief.

title: A Choir of Angels Glorified That Hour...
text:
I


A choir of angels glorified that hour,

the heavenly vault dissolved in flames.

"Father, why have you abandoned me?

Mother, I beg you, do not weep for me..."


II


Mary Magdalene struck her breast and sobbed.

His beloved disciple stood motionless, his face

petrified.

His mother remained apart. No one looked into

her secret eyes. No one dared.




1940-43
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the two-part crucifixion scene and the silence around the mother's eyes.

title: Crucifixion
text:
I


A choir of angels glorified that hour,

the heavenly vault dissolved in flames.

"Father, why have you abandoned me?

Mother, I beg you, do not weep for me..."



II


Mary Magdalene struck her breast and sobbed.

His beloved disciple stood motionless, his face

petrified.

His mother remained apart. No one looked into

her secret eyes. No one dared.




1940-43
editorial_note: The titled variant preserves the crucifixion tableau and the untouchable solitude of the mother.

title: How Can You Look at the Neva?
text:
How can you look at the Neva¹,

how can you stand upon the bridges?

It does not matter if people think I suffer,

His Image will not let me go.

The wings of black angels can do one in,

but I count the days until the Last Judgment.

The streets are stained with eerie pyres,

bonfires of roses in the snow.




1914


1. Neva: Russian river that crosses the city of Saint Petersburg
editorial_note: The translation keeps the Neva footnote, apocalyptic counting, and roses burning in snow.

title: The Word Fell Like a Stone...
text:
The word fell like a stone

onto my living breast.

I confess it: I was prepared

and somehow ready for the trial.

So much to do today:

kill memory, murder pain,

turn the heart to stone

and still get ready to live again.


There is no silence. The feast of warm summer

brings rumors of revelry.

How long had I been foreseeing

this radiant day, this empty house?
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sentence-like blow and the impossible chores of survival.

title: Now No One Will Want to Listen to Songs
text:
Now no one will want to listen to songs.

The bitter prophesied days come from the hill.

I tell you, song, the world has no wonders now;

do not tear my heart apart, learn to stay still.


Not long ago, free as any swallow,

you struggled; happily against the mornings, defying

their dangers.

Now you will wander like a hungry beggar,

desperately knocking at strangers' doors.




1917
editorial_note: The translation preserves the address to song as a once-free creature reduced to begging.

title: We Are So Intoxicated with Each Other
text:
We are so intoxicated with each other

that suddenly we could be shipwrecked,

this incomparable paradise

could become a terrible affliction.

Everything has drawn near to crime;

God must forgive us.

Despite infinite patience,

forbidden roads have crossed.

We carry paradise like a blessed chain.

We gaze into it, as into an unfathomable cistern,

deeper than the admirable books

that suddenly arise and contain everything.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the love-paradise as both blessing, chain, and forbidden crossing.

title: The Poet
text:
You think this is work, this carefree life:

to hear something from music and call it yours as if nothing.

And to slip another's playful scherzo into crafty verses,

swearing that the poor heart groans in luminous fields.

And to hear something from the forest and watch the taciturn pines

while the misty curtain of fog rises everywhere.

I take, far away or beside me, feeling no guilt in my turn,

a little of crafty life and the rest from nocturnal silence.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's ironic account of borrowing from music, forest, life, and silence.
